The wage gap doesn't really exist. Women make within 5-10% of men, which can easily be explained by other (non-discriminatory) factors that simply can't all be taken into account with current models. Young American women now make more than young American men in urban areas, with the opposite being true in rural areas, and it's easy to understand why that would be.

There are some discrepancies that should be addressed, like the educational system's hostility to males and the assumption that women are inferior employees, but the pros and cons seem to weigh equally for the genders, even if they aren't the same across genders.

This is a complex issue and I don't know if it'll ever be a way to satisfactorily "debunk" the wage gap myth. There are SO many qualitative factors that affect pay. I always think more women will step out of the workforce to raise children and it can be very difficult to recover from that in terms of salary equality. Most workplaces still don't have adequate flexibility to allow parents to schedule their professional lives around their personal lives. My office has a very weak telework policy and an employe survey found that women were overwhelmingly denied the right to telecommute while men were given greater latitude in that privilege. Managers expressed doubts that women would actually be caring for their children when they were supposed to be working remotely. Of course they assumed that men would be working. This double standard resulted in a lot of women leaving this firm, or just not accepting promotions so they could spend more time caring for family.

Anecdotally, I also know a lot of women who have accepted lower paying positions in exchange for increased flexibility and the expectation that they'd be required to put in fewer overtime hours. If a woman accepts this position, while a man opts for an identical position (but he's expected to put in longer hours, etc.), how does this factor into the pay gap?

I wish the salary discrimination bill would have passed, making discussion of salary a non-fireable offense. If you lay it all out on the table in the open, it's pretty hard to support the myths around it.
